title: Texas Hold'em Starting Hands: A Guide for Canadians
excerpt: Learn which Texas Hold'em starting hands to play, which to fold and how position and stack depth change your choices at Canadian online poker tables.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
Starting hand selection is the single most important habit separating winning Texas Hold'em players from losing ones, and it is also one of the easiest to improve. Many Canadian players who sit down at an online table play far too many hands, hoping to catch a flop. Learning which hands to play, which to fold and how position changes everything will tighten your game and protect your bankroll. This guide gives you a practical framework for Texas Hold'em starting hands, whether you play cash games, sit-and-gos or tournaments.

Why starting hands matter

Texas Hold'em gives each player two private cards, and the decision to play or fold them is the first and cheapest you will make on every hand. Folding costs nothing beyond the blind you have already posted. Playing a weak hand costs money, and it often puts you in difficult spots after the flop where you are guessing rather than choosing.

Strong players are selective. They enter fewer pots, but when they do, they usually hold a hand with good equity and a clear plan. Over thousands of hands, this selectivity is what turns small edges into steady results.

The main categories of starting hands

It helps to group hands into types rather than memorizing a chart of 169 combinations. The categories below give you a mental shortcut at the table.

  • Premium pairs: pocket aces, kings, queens and jacks are strong in almost any situation and are usually worth raising.
  • Big suited and offsuit cards: hands like ace-king and ace-queen dominate many opponents and play well both pre-flop and after the flop.
  • Medium pairs: pairs from tens down to sevens or so have solid value, especially for set mining and in later position.
  • Suited connectors: hands like jack-ten suited or nine-eight suited can make straights and flushes, and they gain value in position and with deep stacks.
  • Small pairs and weak aces: these are often marginal and best played only in the right position and against the right opponents.

Why suited and connected hands gain value

Suited cards add flush potential, and connected cards add straight potential. Together they make hands that can win big pots without needing to be the best hand on the flop. However, they are speculative, so they work best when it is cheap to see a flop and when you have position on your opponents.

Position changes your range

The same two cards can be a fold in one seat and a raise in another. Acting later in a hand gives you more information, because you see what opponents do before you decide. That advantage is why the button is the most profitable seat at the table. Our guide on poker position and why the button wins explores this idea in depth.

As a rule, play tighter from early position, where many players still have to act behind you, and loosen up gradually as you move toward the button and the cutoff. In early position, stick largely to premium pairs and strong broadway hands. On the button, you can add more suited connectors, smaller pairs and a wider range of ace-x suited hands.

Facing a raise

When someone raises before you, your range should usually narrow. A hand you would happily open with may be a fold against an early-position raise, because that player likely holds a strong range. Hands that dominate easily, such as ace-jack against ace-ten, can lose big pots, so be careful with dominated hands in raised pots.

Stack depth and game type

The right starting hands also depend on how deep the stacks are. With deep stacks, speculative hands like suited connectors gain value because the potential winnings are large compared with the cost of seeing a flop. With short stacks, high-card strength and pairs matter more, because there is less room to outplay opponents after the flop.

Tournament play adds another layer. As blinds rise and stacks shrink, ranges change, and push-or-fold decisions become more common. Cash games and tournaments reward different adjustments, so a hand that is a comfortable call in a deep-stacked cash game might be a fold near a tournament bubble.

Common mistakes to avoid

The most common error among newer players is playing too many hands because they feel bored or hope to get lucky. Another is overvaluing any ace, even a weak one, when kicker strength matters. A third is calling raises with hands that are rarely best, such as low suited cards in out-of-position seats.

Fixing these leaks does not require complicated study. It requires patience and a willingness to fold more than feels comfortable. Many players find that simply folding more marginal hands improves their results within a few sessions.

Avoid results-based thinking

It is tempting to judge a decision by its outcome. A weak hand that happens to win a big pot can reinforce a bad habit. Instead, ask whether the decision was sound given the position, stack sizes and opponents. Over a large sample, good decisions win out, even though any single hand can go either way.

Practising and improving

Start with low-stakes tables where mistakes are cheap. Keep a note of hands you were unsure about and review them later. Many players also use study tools to compare their choices with sound ranges, though you should check each site's rules on which tools are permitted. If you are new to the rules, our poker game guide covers hand rankings and betting rounds, and Ontario players can see regulated options on our operator reviews page.

Remember that poker is a long game. Bankroll management is part of selection too: playing stakes that are too high for your funds forces you into bad decisions because you cannot afford variance. Keep your buy-ins comfortably within your budget, and move up only when you have a cushion.

A quick pre-flop routine

Before you act, ask yourself three questions. What is my position? What has happened in front of me? How deep are the stacks? Answering these will usually point to a clear decision. Over time the routine becomes automatic, freeing your attention for reading opponents and planning your play after the flop.

Good starting hand selection will not guarantee wins, because luck always plays a part in Texas Hold'em. But it gives you a lasting edge, reduces costly guesswork and makes the game more enjoyable. Play within your means and treat poker as a skill-based form of entertainment.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
